questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273713/assets/6f34d18ec0aed1f28e77a143c5be0b3d4eaf44ba08649d02517c6c6ea5bc0af4.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k-x.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (k-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(0)-\frac{(0)^{2}}{2}+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8.
$$

Finally, since $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =kx-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(2)-\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+8 \\ 12 & =2k+6 \\ 2k & =6 \\ k & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273713/assets/2d768dd32288c71332e81b0f72aa2652c19a7c80fed6751abea5ced383e6848f.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(3-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(3-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(3-x) & =0 \\ 3-x & =0 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=3\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,3)$ | $3$ | $(3,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $4$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $k>0$ | $0$ | $-k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=3\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(3-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(3-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=4\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(3(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{6})^{2} & =k(3(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{2})+8 \\ 12 & =4k+8 \\ 4k & =4 \\ k & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =1(3x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+8 \\ {v}^{2} & =6x-{x}^{2}+16 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+6x+16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+6x+16}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(3)=\sqrt{-(3)^{2}+6(3)+16}=5\,m/s
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(2x-\frac{1}{2})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $1\,m/s$ when its displacement is $1\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273713/assets/6046ef89f9abcc78be695d69df64471fb9c68645473c946e7f3212be27e2c6fb.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x-\frac{1}{2})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2x-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2x-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (2x-\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=1\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =(1)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}(1)+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & ={x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x(x-\frac{1}{2}) & =0 \\ x & =0\,m,\,\frac{1}{2}\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is ${x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $2\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\sqrt[3]{7}\,m,$ find the values of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273713/assets/1b474c320ec59107dd191ab4420f0d4edb1e551164d90b741338da1e0dd3b23d.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is ${x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={x}^{2}.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})={x}^{2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=\sqrt[3]{7}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{1}{3}(\sqrt[3]{7})^{3}+C \\ C & =2-\frac{7}{3} \\ C & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{{x}^{3}-1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{3}-1}{3} \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =\frac{{x}^{3}-1}{3} \\ {x}^{3}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =1 \\ x & =1\,m.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(kx+6)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=19\,m/s$ when its displacement is $8\,m,$ find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14273713/assets/f7468aaa11c79f4306b67a558f09cbf5d8a6a480b726e883ecb373d7e5660e37.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(kx+6)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=kx+6.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=kx+6.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (kx+6)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+6x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=3\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+6x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(3)^{2} & =\frac{k(0)^{2}}{2}+6(0)+C \\ C & =\frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+6x+\frac{9}{2}.
$$

Finally, since $v=19\,m/s$ when $x=8\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{k{x}^{2}}{2}+6x+\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}(19)^{2} & =\frac{k(8)^{2}}{2}+6(8)+\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{361}{2} & =32k+48+\frac{9}{2} \\ 32k & =128 \\ k & =4.\end{aligned}
$$
